analysis.one_liner: Lets each state cap interest rates and fees on consumer loans made to its residents.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in March 2014 and saw no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, national banks and other lenders can 'export' interest rates from their home state, so a lender in a state with no rate cap can charge that rate even in states that cap it. This bill amends the Truth in Lending Act to say the maximum annual percentage rate on a consumer loan, including fees, is the cap set by the state where the borrower lives. Home mortgages are excluded. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers in states with interest rate caps, especially people taking payday loans, installment loans, or carrying credit card balances, who would no longer be charged rates from a lender's home state that exceed their own state's cap. Fees would count toward the cap, closing the workaround of loading costs into 'fees' rather than interest.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers in states with rate caps

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on any consumer credit transaction at the maximum allowed by the borrower's home state, counting fees toward that cap, and overrides other federal law that would permit higher rates.
The cap applies to payday, installment, and credit card lending alike; only residential mortgage transactions are carved out.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer lenders who rely on charging above a state's cap — payday lenders, high-rate installment lenders, and card issuers that export rates from states without caps — would lose that pricing power. Some borrowers with poor credit might see fewer or costlier credit options as lenders pull back in capped states.

drawbacks.text: In states that set no cap at all, the bill changes nothing — it does not create a federal rate ceiling, it only defers to whatever each state chooses, so protection is uneven.
Tighter caps can shrink access to credit for high-risk borrowers: if a lender cannot price for the risk at all, it may not lend, which an honest supporter would acknowledge as a real trade-off.
Excluding residential mortgages leaves the largest consumer debt untouched, so the bill would not restrain home lending costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers in capped states, the bill targets the main workaround that lets lenders sidestep state rate limits: charging the rate of a friendlier home state and packing costs into fees. The cost side is real — stricter caps can mean less credit for people with the worst credit scores — but the bill is modest by design, since it sets no federal ceiling and simply lets each state's existing law apply.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tierney (D-MA) introduced the bill on March 6, 2014, with two Democratic cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction.
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral; the bill died in committee when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer lenders that charge rates above state caps — payday lenders, high-rate installment lenders, and card issuers exporting rates from capless states — kept the status quo, and borrowers in capped states kept paying whatever those lenders charge.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-rate consumer lenders kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. John Tierney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let each state cap rates on loans to its own residents.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or vote on the bill after referral; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the full chamber was never tested.

industries.note: These lenders depend on charging rates well above what most state caps allow, often through out-of-state charters. The bill would let a borrower's home state cap apply, including fees, cutting into their core business model.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and national banks
industries.note: Card issuers currently export rates from their home state, so the bill would force them to honor rate caps in capped states — but in most states their standard rates are legal anyway, so the hit is limited to high-rate cards and fee-heavy products.
Residential mortgages are expressly excluded, so the bill leaves this industry's pricing untouched.
